Received 16 July 2024 l Revised 6 January 2024 l Accepted 12 January 2024 l Published online 14 May 2025 Abstract: Objective: This study investigated the impact of board games on social skills development among at-risk children diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in upper elementary schools in Thailand. Material and Methods: This quasi-experimental study involved at-risk students with ADHD from Wat Tham Nava School and Wat Puech Nimit School. Each group consisted of 44 students, selected based on the Student Behavior Assessment Scale. The sample size was calculated using G*Power software, with participants purposefully assigned to either the control group or the experimental group. The primary intervention was a board game program specifically designed to enhance social skills. Outcome evaluation tools included a social skills questionnaire and a social behavior interview. Data analysis was conducted using descriptive statistics, paired sample t-tests, and independent sample t-tests to assess the effectiveness of the intervention. Results: The experimental group demonstrated significantly higher social skills scores compared to the control group (p-value<0.001), with mean scores of 39.66±3.227 and 7.36±3.596, respectively, indicating the effectiveness of the board game program in enhancing the social skills of at-risk children with ADHD. Remark: Picture Guessing Game Activity Description: Each team collaborates with two to three members from other teams. The team performs poses based on a prepared picture (without using sound) provided by the activity facilitator. The other teams guess the correct pose corresponding to the picture. There are 15 pictures in total, and the activity is timed for two minutes. Stand Firm Game Activity Description: Each person in the team stands on a piece of paper provided by the activity facilitator. The facilitator times the activity for 15 seconds. Ball Passing Game Activity Description: Within the team, participants pass a ball under their legs until it reaches the last person while being timed for 15 seconds. Ping Pong Spoon Relay Activity Description: Within the team, participants carry a ping pong ball on a spoon and place it into a bucket. Five balls are prepared by the activity facilitator. The activity is timed for three minutes. Charades Guessing Game Activity Description: Each team collaborates with two to three members from other teams. The team members mime actions (without using sound) based on clues provided by the activity facilitator. Other teams guess the correct actions corresponding to the clues. There are seven clues in total, with a time limit of two minutes per clue, and a total of 15 clues prepared. Jigsaw Square Geometry Activity Description: Within the team, members assemble jigsaw pieces into various square-shaped geometric patterns provided by the activity facilitator. The activity is timed for three minutes. Three-legged Balloon Race Activity Description: Each team collaborates with fi ve members from another team. The teams pair up with each other, and both members of the pair hold a balloon between their heads and race to a designated spot marked by the activity facilitator. The activity is timed for one minute. Word Relay Game Activity Description: The researchers provide a word to the fi rst person in a team. This word is then passed along the line, and the last person must say the word exactly as it was given to the fi rst person. Spot the Diff erence Game Activity Description: The researchers prepare two images. The fi rst image is complete, while the second image has some missing parts. The team’s task is to fi nd the diff erences within three minutes. What’s Your Name Activity Description: Each team must greet and introduce themselves to another team. They must then remember the names of the members of that team within fi ve minutes. Move the Object Game Activity Description: Each team uses the equipment provided by the facilitator to move a water bottle to a designated spot within fi ve minutes. Draw on the Back Game Activity Description: Each team must draw a picture based on a word provided by the facilitator. Team members line up and draw the picture on each other’s backs. The last person in the line must guess what the drawing is within two minutes. JSON: Name: board_games_social_skills_adhd Title: Effectiveness of a structured board-game intervention for improving social skills in at-risk upper-elementary students with ADHD: a controlled quasi-experimental evaluation Short Hypothesis: Participation in an 8-week structured board-game program causes greater improvement in standardized social skills scores among at-risk upper-elementary students with ADHD compared to standard school activities. Related Work: Existing approaches to improving social skills in children with ADHD include pharmacotherapy combined with behavioral therapy, therapist-led play therapy, and school-based structured activities. Play-based interventions and collaborative games have been reported to improve interpersonal interaction, conflict management, and teamwork, but prior studies commonly suffer from small sample sizes, non-randomized or single-site designs, short intervention periods, and reliance on single-source outcome measures (teacher or self-report). Active-control comparisons are rare; fidelity monitoring and prespecified subscale analyses are often missing. Many studies do not disaggregate effects on specific social skill domains (conflict management, interpersonal, teamwork) and provide limited follow-up data to assess durability. Cultural and implementation differences (type of games, facilitator training, session dose) are poorly characterized, limiting generalizability and reproducibility. Abstract: Problem: At-risk children with ADHD frequently exhibit deficits in social competence that impair school functioning. Approach: Implement and evaluate an 8-week structured board-game program delivered twice weekly to upper-elementary students screened as at-risk for ADHD. Primary outcome assessment uses a validated 15-item social skills questionnaire with subscales for conflict management, interpersonal skills, and teamwork; baseline ADHD risk is confirmed with the SNAP-IV. Main contribution: A controlled experimental pipeline that specifies participant screening, standardized intervention content, fidelity monitoring, and quantitative analysis comparing the board-game intervention to standard school activities and to an active non-social-games control. Expected outcome: The board-game intervention will produce statistically and clinically meaningful improvements in total social skills and subscale scores immediately post-intervention and at a 3-month follow-up, with effect sizes large enough to inform school-based implementation decisions. The pipeline enables replication, domain-specific effect estimation, and objective assessment of intervention fidelity and adverse events. Experiments: Participants: N=88 upper-elementary students (grades 4–6) screened as at-risk for ADHD using SNAP-IV above teacher-defined cutoffs; 44 per arm. Design: two-arm controlled trial (board-game intervention vs standard school activities). Optional 3-arm variant for sensitivity: (1) board-game intervention, (2) active control (non-social recreational games matched for time and facilitator contact), (3) passive control (standard activities). Intervention: structured board-game sessions twice weekly, 2 hours per session, for 8 weeks; standardized activity manual and facilitator training; fidelity logs per session. Outcome measures and timepoints: primary outcome = change in total social skills questionnaire score (15 items) from baseline to immediate post-intervention (week 8); secondary outcomes = changes in subscale scores (conflict management, interpersonal, teamwork), teacher-rated social behavior interview, responder rate (≥20% improvement), Cronbach alpha for questionnaire reliability, and adverse events; assessments at baseline, week 8, and 3-month follow-up. Baselines: standard school activities; active-control recreational program. Evaluation metrics: mean change, 95% CI, Cohen's d, mixed-effects linear model for group*time interaction with participant as random intercept and school as cluster effect, ANCOVA adjusting for baseline score, paired t-tests for within-group changes, chi-square for responder rates, Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple secondary comparisons. Sample size justification: effect size d=0.817, alpha=0.05, power=0.95 yields n≈44 per group. Missing data: multiple imputation and intention-to-treat analysis. Ablation/comparison studies: (A) full board-game program vs board-game program without cross-team collaboration elements (teamwork-removed ablation) to isolate teamwork contribution; (B) dose-response: compare standard frequency (2x/week) to reduced frequency (1x/week) in a randomized subcohort. Pre-registered analysis plan with primary endpoint at week 8. Risk Factors and Limitations: Non-random assignment or cluster confounding if schools are used as arms; selection bias from teacher-based screening; measurement bias from teacher-reported outcomes and social desirability; small sample size limiting detection of subgroup effects and precision of effect estimates; short follow-up restricting assessment of durability; contamination between groups if students interact across arms; facilitator variability and fidelity drift affecting internal validity; concurrent treatments (medication, psychotherapy) confounding effects unless controlled or stratified; cultural specificity of games and instruments limiting generalizability beyond Thai upper-elementary contexts; reliance on a single primary questionnaire (single-instrument measurement risk); attrition and missing data reducing power; overestimation of effect size in initial power calculation leading to underpowered replication; logistical scalability constraints (session time, trained facilitators) for broader implementation.
